Jun 2024 exam: full worked solutions

How to use this: sit it timed first (120 min, open book). Do not open this until time is up.

The paper is “Resources/eec jun24 exam.pdf” (Electric Energy Conversion, Semester 1 2024, W.L. Soong). The course gives numerical answers only (“eec jun24 exam numerical answers”). This pack is the full solution set. Every number below was recomputed in Python and checked against those answers. Where my value differs in the last digit, the note says why.

Marking: each part’s total is the official one from the paper’s cover table. The split inside a part (“1 mark for …”) is my suggested allocation, built the way a marker usually awards method and answer marks. Be strict: give yourself a mark only if your script shows the line that earns it.

Figures: the paper’s own figures are reproduced under each question. They confirm the values used below:

  • Q1c: series and (the same values that the official answers give: W and VAr at 2 A).
  • Q1d: a series RL load with the capacitor across the supply.
  • Q2b: a 15 Ω series resistor, then a 6:1 ideal transformer, then a 0.3 Ω load.
  • Q3a: three torque–speed curves. Top to bottom they are synchronous, DC and induction, as the answer sheet says.

All phasors are rms. is the angle of the current relative to the voltage, so lagging means .

Exam technique for this paper

Time. 120 min for 80 marks is 1.5 min per mark. Budget about 28 min per question and keep 8 min spare. Write the budget for each part next to it in the first minute (for example, 3c [10] = 15 min).

Order of attack. Every question is 20 marks, so start where you are fastest.

  1. Q1 (Ch1–2) and Q2 (Ch3) first. They are the most practised material, from the quiz and test. Bank about 35 of the 40 marks in 55 min.
  2. Q3 next. 3b and 3c are plug-in induction-machine calculations. 3c alone is 10 marks.
  3. Q4 last. 4a and 4b are short per-unit phasor sums. Do not leave 4c (9 marks) to the final 3 minutes. Words-only answers earn marks quickly, about one solid point per mark.

Paper-specific habits that earn marks here.

  • Three-phase means per-phase. Q1b, Q2c, Q3b, Q3c and Q4a all have line values. Divide the line voltage by (star), and divide three-phase power by 3, before you use any per-phase formula. Write “assume star” if the question does not say.
  • Signs carry marks. in Q1d. , , , and are all negative in Q3c (generator). Leading means pf in Q4b.
  • Read which value the part uses. Q1c(ii) and Q1d(iii) each give new data. Do not carry over the earlier current or .
  • Units asked for. Q4a(i) asks for in per-unit, not ohms. Q1d(iii) asks for capacitance in μF.
  • Words only in Q4c. No sketches or equations. Name the effect, the circuit element that models it, and how it varies.
  • Open book. Tab your notes at: back-emf equation and (Ch3), the induction equivalent circuit and power flow (Ch7), and and (Ch8). Do not spend exam time reading theory. Look up a formula, then go.

Increasing the input power for the same power loss would cause the efficiency to ________ (choose decrease or increase).

Ch4–7.

3a) Torque vs. Speed Characteristics [6 marks]

Consider the torque versus speed curves shown in the figure below.

i) For each curve, write the type of machine in the space below the curve and draw the resulting torque curve if the no-load/synchronous speed was reduced to half of its original value. [ 3 marks ]

ii) Alongside each curve, indicate how you could halve the no-load/synchronous speed while ensuring safe machine operation. [ 3 marks ]

Solution

The answer sheet names the curves, in order: synchronous, DC, induction (Lecture Sections 4.1 and 7.9).

(i) [3] Name and sketch.

  1. Synchronous machine: a vertical line at . Halved, it becomes a vertical line at .
  2. DC machine: a straight line falling from at . Halved, it is a parallel line starting at . The slope () is unchanged.
  3. Induction machine: zero torque at , a steep, nearly linear region just below , a peak () and then the starting torque at . Halved at constant V/f, the curve keeps its shape and shifts left to start at . The slip speed at a given torque and the peak torque are unchanged.

(ii) [3] How to halve the speed safely.

  • Synchronous: halve , which halves . Also halve , so that V/f (and hence the peak flux) stays constant. Otherwise the core saturates and the current becomes very large.
  • DC: halve the armature voltage . The no-load speed is .
  • Induction: halve both and (constant V/f), for the same reason as the synchronous machine.

AC machines need a variable-voltage, variable-frequency inverter for this. A DC machine needs a variable DC supply.

Marks: (i) 1 per machine for the correct name and halved curve. (ii) 1 per machine. For the AC machines the mark needs both and .

Common mistake: “halve ” alone for the AC machines. The question says “safe”, and the mark is for keeping V/f constant. Another error is drawing the halved DC line through the origin, or with a different slope.

4c) Short-Answer Questions [9 marks]

Answer the following questions using words only (that is, without using any sketches, drawings or equations).

These model answers are built from the official answer sheet. The sheet says you do not need every point for full marks. Aim for one solid point per mark.

4c(i) [3 marks]. We have discussed three types of electric power: real, reactive and apparent. Explain briefly what each one is and their practical significance.

Model answer
  • Real power comes from the part of the current that is in phase with the voltage. It is the average value of the instantaneous power. It represents energy flowing one way, from the source to the load, and it is the power that does useful work, such as heat or mechanical output. Resistors absorb it.
  • Reactive power comes from the part of the current that is a quarter-cycle (90 degrees) out of phase with the voltage. Its average is zero: energy surges back and forth between the source and the inductors or capacitors each cycle. It does no useful work, but it still adds to the current, and so to the losses and voltage drops. Inductors absorb it and capacitors generate it.
  • Both real and reactive power are scalar quantities.
  • Apparent power is the magnitude of the complex power, whose real part is the real power and whose imaginary part is the reactive power. It is the rms voltage times the total rms current. It sets the current that generators, transformers and cables must carry, so equipment is rated in volt-amperes.

Marks: 1 per power type, for its definition plus its practical significance.

Common mistake: writing or drawing a triangle. The question forbids equations and sketches. Another is saying reactive power “is wasted”. It is not consumed. It oscillates, and its cost is the extra current.

4c(ii) [3 marks]. Consider a transformer operating from an AC supply. Carefully explain what are the main types of losses in the transformer, how are they modelled in the simplified equivalent circuit, and how do these vary with output power.

Model answer
  • Copper (winding) loss: resistive heating of the primary and secondary windings by the load current. In the simplified equivalent circuit it is modelled by the series winding resistances (the primary resistance plus the referred secondary resistance). It is proportional to the square of the current, so at constant voltage it rises with the square of the output power. It is small at light load and dominant at full load.
  • Iron (core) loss: hysteresis loss (energy to repeatedly reverse the magnetisation of the steel) and eddy-current loss (currents induced in the core laminations by the alternating flux). It is modelled by the core-loss resistance in parallel across the supply. It depends on the supply voltage and frequency, through the peak flux density, and not on the load, so it is essentially constant with output power.
  • As a result, efficiency is low at light load. It peaks at the load where the copper loss equals the iron loss.

Marks: 1 for the copper loss mechanism and model, 1 for the iron loss mechanism and model, 1 for how each varies with output.

Common mistake: putting the core loss in series, or saying iron loss rises with load. Also forgetting that the question asks “how do these vary”: give both trends explicitly.

4c(iii) [3 marks]. Carefully explain why the input current of an induction machine under no-load conditions is not zero. What are the physical effects which cause this?

Model answer
  • Magnetising current. Even with no load, the stator must set up the rotating magnetic field in the air gap. This needs a magnetising current, which is modelled by the magnetising reactance. An induction machine has an air gap, so its magnetising current is large, typically a quarter to over half of rated current. It is much larger than in a transformer.
  • Core-loss current. The alternating flux causes hysteresis and eddy-current losses in the stator (and rotor) iron. These need an in-phase current component, which is modelled by the core-loss resistance.
  • Mechanical losses. Even unloaded, the rotor must overcome bearing friction and windage (air drag, including the cooling fan). So it runs slightly below synchronous speed. The small slip induces a small rotor current that supplies this power, and the stator copper loss adds a little more.
  • The no-load current is therefore mostly reactive, so the no-load power factor is very low.

Marks: 1 for magnetising current and with the physical reason, 1 for core loss and , 1 for mechanical losses (friction and windage) and the small slip.

Common mistake: saying “the current is zero because there is no load torque”. Also listing only the equivalent-circuit elements without the physical cause: the answer sheet asks for both.
